summary: This document gives implementers guidelines for MPLS forwarding and a basis for evaluating forwarding implementations. It highlights practical requirements that are easy to overlook, or that are optional in the standards but are often treated as mandatory by network providers.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7325 collects the MPLS forwarding requirements that network operators expect but that the standards leave open or treat as optional. It explains where early implementations went wrong, then gives buyers a list of questions to ask a supplier and a set of tests to run. It is a checklist, not a specification.

questions: what do providers expect from mpls routers
how do mpls routers handle small packets
what must an mpls router support
subtitle: A checklist of what MPLS routers must really do, and how buyers can test whether they do it.

tldr.problem: The MPLS standards leave many practical requirements optional, so equipment suppliers and network operators often disagree about what a router must handle and how fast.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7325 lists the forwarding requirements operators rely on, including arbitrarily deep label stacks, full rate handling of small packets, multipath hashing, denial of service protection and operations support, then gives questions to ask a supplier and tests to run.
tldr.outcome: The document is a shared reference for three audiences: the people who build forwarding hardware, the people who design systems from it, and the people who run the network. It introduces no new requirements of its own, and it warns that the list of pitfalls is probably incomplete.

today: RFC 7325 is an Informational RFC published in August 2014, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It remains a reference document rather than a specification: it collects requirements from other specifications and adds advice, and it says openly that the set of pitfalls it lists is likely to be incomplete.

sections.title: What This Document Is For
sections.content:
The document started as a reply to concerns raised on the MPLS working group mailing list about shortcomings in real implementations. Its purpose is to give implementers guidelines and to give a basis on which forwarding implementations can be evaluated. It highlights the requirements that are easy to miss, or that are optional for conformance but that providers treat as mandatory.

The scope is MPLS forwarding, base pseudowire forwarding and MPLS operations, administration and maintenance. The use of the pseudowire Control Word and of the pseudowire Sequence Number are discussed. Pseudowire Attachment Circuit, Native Service Processing and specific pseudowire applications such as particular forms of VPN are out of scope, as are implementation details, tunnelling encapsulations that carry MPLS, and the use of IP protocol fields other than the address, protocol number and UDP and TCP port numbers in multipath load balancing. The document assumes that forwarding runs in specialised hardware rather than on a general-purpose processor, and that most interfaces operate at 1 Gb/s or more.

It is aimed at three groups: implementers building MPLS forwarding in silicon or software, system designers assembling a forwarding system, and deployers running an MPLS network. The stated purposes are to explain what to do with a deep label stack, to highlight pitfalls when building a forwarding chip, to provide a checklist of features and performance figures to request, and to provide a set of tests to perform. The document is Informational, so its advice may be ignored, but implementers are told to weigh the risk of doing so.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a checklist for people who buy, build and run MPLS routers. It says which requirements operators expect even though the standards leave them optional, and it warns that the list of pitfalls it holds is probably not complete. Its advice is not mandatory, but the document asks implementers to think about the risk of ignoring it.

sections.title: Label Stacks and Common Misconceptions
sections.content:
Early forwarding silicon made several assumptions about MPLS that later proved wrong, and the document corrects them. The first is that a label stack is shallow. There are practical reasons to have more than one or two labels, and under some circumstances the stack becomes quite deep. The label stack must be treated as arbitrarily deep: RFC 3031 states that the mechanism allows LSP tunnelling to nest to any depth, so if the bottom of the stack cannot be found but enough labels exist to forward the packet, the router must forward it and must not assume the packet is malformed unless the end of the packet is found first. Deep stacks are not rare in networks that meet them, and full packet rate performance is required regardless of stack depth, except where multiple pop operations are required.

Stacks get deep through ordinary combinations. Carrying LDP tunnels inside RSVP-TE tunnels needs a minimum of two labels. Fast reroute adds one more, so at least three labels are present on links traversed by the bypass path. Adding a VPN service brings the depth to four, and MPLS hierarchy can add at least one more. Theoretically eight or more labels are possible, and other uses of the label stack, such as source routing, could go deeper still.

The second misconception concerns small packets. Long bursts of short packets with 40-byte or 44-byte IP payloads are common, caused by TCP acknowledgement compression. A forwarding engine should, if practical, sustain an arbitrarily long sequence of small packets arriving at full interface rate. If that is not practical, the engine must at least buffer a long sequence of small packets before the decision engine and sustain full interface rate for a reasonable average packet rate, because without that buffering, packets are dropped regardless of their quality of service marking.

The document also states that implementations must support the pseudowire Control Word where MPLS-TP or the Associated Channel Header is in use, and should support it otherwise, so that multipath in the underlying network does not disturb pseudowire traffic. Implementers should support adding a pseudowire Flow Label and an MPLS Entropy Label, though deployments may leave them off. Finally, it warns against treating non-IETF definitions of MPLS as normative texts, citing RFC 5704, which records the incompatibilities that produced significant problems in one such specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Two early assumptions were wrong. The first was that a packet carries only one or two MPLS labels; in practice tunnels nest inside tunnels, and a router must handle a stack of any depth. The second was that a router only has to keep up with average traffic; in reality long bursts of very small packets are common, and a router that cannot hold them in a small buffer drops them before it can even read their priority marking.

sections.title: Packet Rates and the Small-Packet Burst
sections.content:
Average packet sizes on the Internet are large, but long sequences of small packets have been both predicted and observed. Traffic compression and TCP acknowledgement compression conspire to produce long runs of packets with 40 to 44 bytes of payload. Over Ethernet the 64-byte minimum frame applies, which gives a packet rate of about 150 million packets per second for the duration of the burst on a nominal 100 Gb/s link; for other encapsulations the peak rate can be as high as 250 million packets per second, for example when IP or MPLS is carried using GFP over OTN ODU4.

A rate that is acceptable for one packet size can be unacceptable for the next. A graph of packet rate against packet size often shows a sawtooth, commonly caused by a memory bottleneck and memory widths, sometimes an internal cache and often a very wide external buffer memory interface, and sometimes by a fabric transfer width. Fine packing, rounding up to the nearest 8 or 16 bytes, gives a fine sawtooth with small degradation for 65-byte packets and less for 82-byte packets; coarse packing, rounding up to 64 bytes, can give a sharper drop.

The loss of some TCP acknowledgements is not the main concern. When a burst arrives, any other packets are dropped once the on-chip input buffers in front of the decision engine are exceeded, and those buffers are often very small or nonexistent, which causes drops that ignore quality of service entirely. For this reason, hardware that cannot process minimum-size packets at full line rate must be able to handle large bursts of small packets instead. Without this performance, packets are lost before their DSCP or MPLS Traffic Class field can even be inspected.

With adequate on-chip buffers in front of the decision engine, a router can absorb a long sequence of short packets and deal with them according to their configured treatment rather than dropping them at random. The buffer should hold many small packets, a few large packets, and a mixture of sizes. These buffers need not add much delay, because they are only used when the decision engine falls behind. The example given is a buffer for 4K packets of 64 bytes, or 256KB, which corresponds to 200 microseconds on a 10 Gb/s link and 20 microseconds on a 100 Gb/s link. If the decision engine can handle small packets at 90 percent of the full rate, the added delay is at most 20 microseconds and 2 microseconds respectively, and only when a burst of short packets occurs.
sections.plainLanguage: A 100 Gb/s link carrying nothing but the smallest possible packets must forward about 150 million packets per second, and a burst of them can last long enough to overwhelm a router that is not built for it. The fix is a small buffer inside the router that holds the burst until the forwarding logic catches up. That buffer adds only tens of microseconds of delay, and only while a burst is happening.

sections.title: Multipath and Load Balancing
sections.content:
Large providers use hash-based multipath in the core and at the edge, and often in metro networks as well. Packets within a microflow, meaning the packets of one flow, should not be reordered, and service providers usually impose the stronger rule that they must not be reordered except in rare circumstances. The common techniques are Equal-Cost Multipath at the IP forwarding level, Ethernet link aggregation with inspection of the IP payload, and multipath on links carrying both IP and MPLS, where the IP header is inspected below the label stack. In most core networks the vast majority of traffic is MPLS encapsulated, so support for multipath is considered essential.

To balance the load properly, information from the IP header must be used. Common practice is to reinspect the IP headers at each router and hash the label stack together with IP header information, using a seed chosen by each router. Where Flow Labels or Entropy Labels are used, a hash seed must be used when creating them.

Several features support this. A pseudowire encapsulated at the network edge needs a means of preventing reordering in the core, and the pseudowire Control Word provides it; not supporting the Control Word may lock a product out of consideration, although it might be enough for applications that are strictly intra-metro and low bandwidth. A pseudowire Flow Label is required only for pseudowires of relatively large capacity, and any pseudowire that uses the Control Word without a Flow Label is in effect a single microflow, which can cause the load-balance problems described in the document. Those problems arise when a few large microflows each consume a large share of a link, because one such flow can upset the balance and more than one can reduce the effective capacity of a composite link by more than 10 percent.

The MPLS Entropy Label simplifies flow group identification at midpoint routers. Before it existed, a midpoint router had to inspect the entire label stack and often the IP headers to distribute traffic adequately. With an Entropy Label, the hash can be performed close to the network edge, placed in the label stack, and used by midpoint routers without reinspecting the stack or the payload. Label stack inspection can stop at the first Entropy Label, which is generally after only a small number of labels. To gain this, a router nearer the edge must be able to add the Entropy Label, which is likely to be required in the edge or border to the core and for routers peering with external networks. The document notes that a generation of edge equipment able to add the Entropy Label is needed before the performance requirements for core routers can be relaxed, and advises not to count on it for now.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks spread traffic over several links by hashing parts of the packet, so that each flow keeps to one path and its packets stay in order. Doing that correctly means reading the IP header under the MPLS labels at every hop, which is slow. The Entropy Label was invented so the hash can be computed once near the edge and carried in the stack, saving the work in the core.

sections.title: What to Ask a Supplier and What to Test
sections.content:
The document gives open-ended questions to put to a supplier, grouped into broad categories, followed by tests that check whether the supplier disclosed its limitations accurately. The compliance questions ask whether packets can be forwarded with an arbitrarily large stack depth and what limits apply, whether the whole set of basic MPLS functionality in Section 2.1 is supported, whether special-purpose labels and extended special-purpose labels are handled correctly and fast enough, whether mappings of label value and Traffic Class to Per-Hop Behavior are handled correctly, whether time synchronisation is supported in forwarding hardware in both PTP and NTP formats, whether link bundling is supported, whether MPLS hierarchy is supported in the pipe, short-pipe and uniform models, whether fast reroute is supported in its one-to-one and facility backup forms and how quickly protection recovers, whether pseudowire Sequence Numbers are handled correctly, and whether VPN edge router functionality is handled without performance problems.

The performance questions ask whether very small packets can be forwarded at full line rate on all interfaces indefinitely and, if not, the smallest packet size at which full rate is possible and the longest burst of full-rate small packets that can be sustained. Other groups cover multipath capabilities and performance, pseudowire capabilities, Entropy Label support, denial of service protection and operations support.

Denial of service protection is called out as an area needing hardware support that is often overlooked. Two protections are usually cited: carrying control and management traffic out of band, which for MPLS means using the Generic Associated Channel and its label, and cryptographic authentication, which stops malicious injection of control traffic but can itself be overwhelmed by a flood of traffic to decrypt. The document is explicit about the order of defence. Isolated control traffic is the first line, filtering, including the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism, is the second, and cryptographic authentication is the last resort and is insufficient on its own against a distributed denial of service attack. At the very minimum, packet filtering, classification and the use of multiple queues supporting rate limiting are needed for traffic that could reach the general-purpose processor.
sections.plainLanguage: The document gives buyers a list of questions to ask a supplier and tests to run against the answer. It also sets the order of defence against a flood of traffic aimed at a router's control processor: keep control traffic out of the payload path, filter what reaches the processor, and treat cryptography as a last resort, because checking signatures at line rate is expensive.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the document reviews forwarding behaviour specified elsewhere and adds compliance and performance requirements, it introduces no new security requirements. It notes that the pitfalls it lists are already widely known in the service provider community and among leading equipment suppliers, and that extreme data and packet rates are needed to affect existing equipment, which makes this kind of denial of service unlikely and undetectable denial of service of this type impossible.

The MPLS security points of the normative references are then summarised. MPLS encapsulation has no authentication extension. The differentiated services documents mention theft of service and denial of service due to mismarking. The OAM control channels defined for the pseudowire Control Word, VCCV and the Generic Associated Channel can be abused. The Generalized TTL Security Mechanism gives protection against high volume spoofing. The BFD payload supports authentication, but the MPLS encapsulation and the control channels that may carry it do not, so IPsec is suggested for securing IP return paths. The MPLS and GMPLS Security Framework and the MPLS-TP security framework treat MPLS as running inside a trusted zone, which is where a single service provider has total operational control.

The document concludes that if control-plane and management-plane security are robust, compromise of one network element may cause chaos in the data plane through denial of service, but not a Byzantine failure in which other elements are fully compromised. End-user applications, including the provider's own control-plane and management-plane protocols, are expected to use end-to-end authentication and, where appropriate, end-to-end encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no rules of its own about security. It repeats the ones that apply to the MPLS specifications it draws on, including that MPLS itself offers no way to authenticate a packet, and that the usual answer is to protect the control and management channels and to use end-to-end encryption for the traffic that matters.

items.title: Equal-Cost Multipath
items.text: Several equal-cost paths at the IP forwarding level.

items.title: Link aggregation
items.text: Several physical links treated as one, with the IP payload inspected.

items.title: Reinspection at each hop
items.text: The router reads the IP header under the labels and hashes it with a local seed.

items.title: Pseudowire Control Word
items.text: Keeps the packets of one pseudowire in order across a multipath core.

items.title: Pseudowire Flow Label
items.text: Lets a large pseudowire be split into several microflows for balancing.

items.title: Entropy Label
items.text: Carries the hash result in the stack so the core need not read the payload.
